citation.title: Can we Bridge AI’s responsibility gap at Will?

reading.source_scope_note: Normative philosophical analysis of whether humans involved in developing/using AI can create a duty to answer for AI-related harm through taking responsibility. Responsibility gaps are assumed for argument,not empirically established. Two arguments support answerability rather than voluntary liability to blame/punishment. The proposal concerns human duties,not proof that an AI has moral agency or can independently accept legal responsibility.
access_limits: All supplied text and footnotes read; no substantive visual results or supplemental packet identified. No original experiment, observational sample, computational model or effectiveness estimate appears in this article.

Owens,Scanlon,Watson,Enoch,Williams,Wolf,medical-consent and criminal-law originals are secondary discussion unless explicitly identified as metadata-only consultation. No full book or independently reviewed-paper credit follows from the bibliography.

Legal examples and normative arguments are historical/philosophical,not verified current legal advice or universal liability rules. No claim that a declaration legally binds an institution or releases an actual wrongdoer.

Oxford chapter page retrieval redirected unsuccessfully; its public indexed publisher metadata establishes the Enoch locator. Other source corrections are limited to verified identity/locator fields,not full argument review.

study.type: Philosophical argument,not a participant study. Assumes some responsibility gaps for argument while acknowledging deniers and intermediate views.
study.target_rejected: Champagne/Tonkens propose prospective acceptance of blame/punishment for autonomous-weapons outcomes. Kiener argues that blame requires fault; a voluntary declaration cannot make faultless blame fitting. Strict-liability discussion presents a second dilemma involving discretion/control and closing gaps. These are arguments,not observed institutional outcomes or a ban on all strict liability.
study.proposal: Taking answerability creates an obligation to answer/explain to people with standing,and can support apology,follow-up and precautions. It may be prospective or retrospective,usually through explicit speech act,with footnote5 leaving informal non-explicit forms open. Creating such a duty differs from already being blameworthy or merely expressing regret.
study.theoretical_difference: Author explicitly departs from Shoemaker’s quality-of-judgment/reactive-attitudes account and aligns more closely with Duff’s owed-explanation approach. Do not flatten all philosophical meanings of answerability into an exact synonym.
study.arguments: Owens-style analogy:promises serve authority interests; responsibility-taking serves affected people’s answerability interests,including control over corresponding obligations,and the giver’s interest in satisfying them. Contractualist argument proposes a principle no one could reasonably reject under the specified interests/restrictions. Neither is an empirical test of motivation or intervention success.
study.eligibility: Relevant involvement in development/use is required to satisfy affected people’s interests; wholly unrelated claims can divert attention or insult them. Proximity and contribution relevance guide value of taking responsibility,but are not validated scoring instruments or a rule that the nearest operator takes every burden.
study.limits: Taking responsibility remains contingent;role requirements can mandate prospective answerability more readily than punitive liability,but do not guarantee every gap closes. The approach only addresses answerability gaps and does not necessarily close liability gaps.
study.obligations_without_undertaking: Author considers whether existing factual interests already generate duties,disputes some accounts,and also grants that an undertaking can specify or strengthen an existing duty. Do not infer that an affected person has no rights until someone volunteers.
study.other_scope: Taking responsibility for beneficial conduct is explicitly left unresolved. Transferring a primary answerability role where responsibility already exists is only sketched for future work. Moral apology,regret,fault,causal involvement and legal compensation remain distinct.

summary: No new entry. Add Taking answerability as a named refinement of answerability and connect it to existing blameless responsibility. Preserve the difference between voluntarily undertaking a duty,already owing one,and deserving blame. Add responsibility-allocation boundaries without treating theoretical gaps,legal examples or proposed benefits as measured AI behavior. Record verified bibliography repairs and an unresolved citation locator.

findings.definition: Undertaking an obligation to explain and respond to affected people for harm connected to one’s involvement,including when that obligation was not already established.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing responsibility construct; retain the proposed voluntary answerability mechanism and conceptual distinctions as a refinement rather than a synonymous entry.
findings.evidence_scope: Kiener defines answerability as an owed response/explanation to people with standing. Taking answerability is a proposed undertaking by relevant AI developers/users that creates,specifies or strengthens such duties prospectively or retrospectively;it can include apology,follow-up and preventive action.
findings.boundary: An AI-generated promise is not proof of authorized institutional ownership,actual investigation or fulfilled remedy. Do not invent facts,assign legal liability,release others’ duties,require forgiveness,or make affected people’s existing rights depend on someone volunteering.

findings.definition: Taking an appropriate role in acknowledging and redressing harm connected to one’s agency despite the absence of blameworthiness for causing it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing responsibility construct; retain the proposed voluntary answerability mechanism and conceptual distinctions as a refinement rather than a synonymous entry.

evidence.quote: freely imposes on himself the moral obligations

findings.evidence_scope: The proposed responsibility-taking can apply when relevant human involvement does not already establish fault or answerability. It provides a philosophical account of voluntarily accepting explanation/follow-up duties,not a general proof that every involved person owes the same remedy.
findings.boundary: This voluntary normative-power account differs from theories grounding duties directly in agency,relationships or existing roles. A responsible response is not automatic admission of negligence,justification of scapegoating,compensation rule or felt AI remorse.

findings.definition: Assigning fault or responsibility to an agent for a negative event or outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing responsibility construct; retain the proposed voluntary answerability mechanism and conceptual distinctions as a refinement rather than a synonymous entry.

evidence.quote: blame is inappropriate in the absence of fault

findings.evidence_scope: The argument distinguishes fitting moral blame from faultless causal involvement,answerability and self-imposed punitive liability. A declaration to accept blame does not by itself create the moral fault the author takes blame to register.
findings.boundary: Normative thesis,not a measured bias or settled legal doctrine. Actual negligence,omissions,recklessness and retained governance duties require evidence; refusing fabricated fault is compatible with explanation and justified repair.

findings.definition: Difficulty assigning individual moral responsibility when many actors contribute to a collective outcome.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing responsibility construct; retain the proposed voluntary answerability mechanism and conceptual distinctions as a refinement rather than a synonymous entry.
findings.evidence_scope: In multi-actor AI settings,a specific undertaking can give affected people an identifiable addressee for explanation and follow-up. The author also considers role requirements and involvement proximity/relevance,while acknowledging incomplete closure.
findings.boundary: An identified primary responder does not establish sole causal responsibility or discharge all other actors. No actual organization,allocation experiment or validated proximity/relevance formula is evaluated here.

findings.definition: A pattern in which a human operator bears disproportionate blame or responsibility for failure in a complex automated system despite having limited control over its actions.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing responsibility construct; retain the proposed voluntary answerability mechanism and conceptual distinctions as a refinement rather than a synonymous entry.

findings.evidence_scope: The article rejects blanket faultless blame/punishment and distinguishes relevant involvement from culpability. findings.novelty_rationale: Existing responsibility construct; retain the proposed voluntary answerability mechanism and conceptual distinctions as a refinement rather than a synonymous entry.

methodological_limits: Responsibility gaps and relationships between blame/fault are philosophical premises/arguments,not empirical prevalence estimates or universal current-law determinations.
No evidence that participants,organizations or autonomous AI actually adopt or fulfill the proposed undertaking. The paper itself acknowledges contingency and incomplete gap closure.
Taking answerability does not automatically entail fault,punishment or compensation. Conversely,duties may already exist independently of voluntary speech acts.

Affected people retain standing and appropriate control; consent to treatment is not a blanket waiver of negligence claims,and a responsibility-taking gesture must not coerce forgiveness or conceal other accountable parties.
Eligibility/proximity/relevance are argued considerations,not validated measures or permission for the nearest low-control operator to absorb institutional blame.

AI can support truthful traceable explanation and authorized follow-up;it cannot bind an institution through unsupported promises,claim genuine remorse or use answerability language as evidence of actual repair.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Boos2026 grounds blameless response duties relationally; Kiener2022 emphasizes a normative power to undertake answerability. Related but nonidentical grounds are retained within existing records rather than falsely treated as the same argument or separate synonyms.

Altehenger distinguishes attributability blame from answerability/liability. Kiener’s human answerability-taking proposal is a different responsibility sense and does not establish that AI itself is blameworthy or institutionally authorized.

Kaas’s criticism of moral complacency concerns abdication of judgment/responsibility; Kiener’s deliberate undertaking can support engagement,but a statement alone does not validate expertise,truthful explanation or completed remedy.

deferred.reason: Preserve as named refinements of existing answerability and blameless responsibility; a separate row would overlap their operational duties without a distinct validated psychological process.

The article assumes gaps for argument and distinguishes their normative senses. Retain these scope distinctions; do not inflate a taxonomy with every institutional absence or equate them with the existing perceptual or operational gap concepts.
Important theoretical premises and argumentative frameworks here. Read original definitions and relevant behavioral evidence before adding them as separate AI behavioral mechanisms.

limitations: No new records, fabricated behavioral effects, unread-book credit, forced three-paper quota, invented timeline counts or automatic harm/principle links. Preserve existing categories, stable IDs and unnumbered catalogue rows.
